question: Assume the JTB definition of Knowledge, which suggests that "Knowledge is a Justified True Belief". If our only available epistemic states are Knowledge and Belief, what are the two problems JTB runs into? Ignore Gettier problems.

6.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The two problems are (i) the infinite regress problem and (ii) the arbitrary-foundation problem. If the only available epistemic states are Knowledge and Belief, then any justified belief must be supported either by another belief or by something known. If it is supported by another belief, that supporting belief needs justification in turn; if it is supported by knowledge, that knowledge itself must already be justified. So the chain either continues indefinitely or it has to stop at some belief accepted without further justification—making the stopping point arbitrary or dogmatic. Thus JTB faces a regress and an arbitrary-foundation problem.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With JTB you have only two live categories.

Knowledge = Justified + True + Belief
Belief = everything else that is still a belief

That means the justification dimension and the truth dimension cannot be tracked independently of knowledge. 

1. Justified belief without truth. A belief can be epistemically good because it is justified even if it happens to be false, e.g. a well-evidenced scientific hypothesis that later turns out false. On JTB it is not knowledge because it is not true, so with only Knowledge and Belief as options it is forced into the undifferentiated category Belief. Justified false belief is therefore indistinguishable from unjustified false belief and the independent epistemic value of justification is lost.

2. True belief without justification. A belief can be epistemically better than a false belief because it is true even if it is held for no good reason, e.g. a lucky guess. On JTB it is not knowledge because it is not justified, so with only Knowledge and Belief as options it is forced into the same undifferentiated category Belief as a false unjustified belief. True unjustified belief is therefore indistinguishable from false unjustified belief and the independent epistemic value of truth is lost.

In short, JTB with only Knowledge and Belief collapses justified false belief and unjustified true belief into bare Belief, so you lose a distinct epistemic state for justified belief simpliciter and for true belief simpliciter.

(2) The problem of arbitrary foundations: to stop the regress, JTB would need some belief to be justified without further support. But with only knowledge and belief available, any such stopping point is either a merely believed foundational item, which is arbitrary, or a piece of knowledge, which cannot serve as a more basic independent justifier. Thus JTB faces either an infinite regress or an arbitrary stopping point.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Under the truth x justification matrix JTB gives you four
cells.

* T & J  → Knowledge
* T & ~J → ?
* ~T & J → ?
* ~T & ~J → ?

With the only labels you are allowed, Knowledge and Belief, the three
non-knowledge cells all have to be called Belief. In effect

Knowledge = True & Justified & Believed
Belief    = everything else = T&~J ∨ ~T&J ∨ ~T&~J

That coarse graining buys the loss of any epistemic discrimination
between the three non-knowledge combinations.

* The justified false belief problem. A ~T&J belief is a good,
warranted belief that happens to be false. On JTB it is not
knowledge, so with only Knowledge/Belief as resources it has to be
put in the same undifferentiated Belief box as ~T&~J unjustified
false belief. The epistemic credit due to justification is lost and
justified false belief is made indistinguishable from arbitrary false
belief.

* The unjustified true belief problem. A T&~J belief is true but
unwarranted, a matter of luck. On JTB it is not knowledge, so with only
Knowledge/Belief it has to be put in the same Belief box as ~T&J
justified false belief and ~T&~J false belief. The epistemic defect of
lack of justification is lost and an accidentally true belief is made
indistinguishable from a justified false belief.

In other words the JTB taxonomy collapses the four truth/justification
combinations into two labels, so Belief becomes a heterogeneous
catch-all for unjustified true belief, justified false belief and
unjustified false belief. You can no longer mark the epistemic
difference between being warranted and being lucky, nor between being
warranted and being unwarranted, which is the usual motivation for
having distinct attitudes between mere belief and knowledge.

If only Knowledge and Belief are available, then any attempt to justify a belief must appeal either to further knowledge or to another belief. Appealing to further knowledge generates an endless chain: each knowledge claim itself needs justification. But if the chain is supposed to end, it must stop at some belief that is accepted without further justification, which is an arbitrary or dogmatic stopping point. Thus JTB faces the regress on one side and the need for an unjustified foundation on the other.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With the three-place matrix True/False x Justified/Unjustified x Belief you get four
belief-cells. JTB labels only one of them Knowledge.

Knowledge = Justified & True & Belief
Belief, as the only residual state, is then identified with not-Knowledge.

That forces a collapse of the truth/justification matrix.

* Justified False Belief. A belief can be well warranted and still false. On JTB it is
not Knowledge because it is not true. With only Knowledge vs Belief as available
labels the state has to be put under Belief, and Belief thereby has to carry the
justification. Justification is thus rendered invisible for false beliefs: justified
false belief is indistinguishable from unjustified false belief. In effect JTB has
no epistemic home for warranted error.

* Unjustified True Belief. A belief can be true by luck, accident, testimony you
have not checked, etc., and be completely unwarranted. On JTB it is not Knowledge
because it is not justified. With only Knowledge vs Belief as available labels the
state has to be put under Belief, so that a true belief is lumped together with
false belief. Truth is thus rendered invisible for non-knowledge beliefs: an
unjustified true belief is indistinguishable from an unjustified false belief.
In effect JTB has no epistemic home for lucky truth.

Hence on a Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy you lose the two intermediate cells
JFB and UTB. Justification and truth can come apart, and JTB has no state in which
to locate the justified but false and the true but unjustified. That is the
conventional justification/truth mismatch that the four-cell account is designed
to avoid, and it is the reason for postulating at least the further epistemic
kinds justified belief and mere true belief in addition to Knowledge and mere
Belief. Gettier cases are a separate difficulty.

5.text:
With JTB the 2x2 of Truth x Justification is

          Justified   Unjustified
True      Knowledge   True belief
False     Justified false belief  False belief

Knowledge is the JTB cell. If the only epistemic kinds you are allowed to
name are Knowledge and Belief, the three other cells have to be packed
into Belief. That packing is counter-intuitive.

* Justified false belief. A belief can be well supported, well justified,
and still false. Intuitively justification is an epistemic good even when
it fails to make the belief true. On JTB a justified false belief is not
knowledge, so with only Knowledge and Belief to name it it has to be
named mere Belief. It is therefore epistemically indistinguishable from an
unjustified false belief, although we want to say the justified false
believer is in a better epistemic position.

* Unjustified true belief. A belief can be true and yet held for bad or
no reasons, a lucky guess. Intuitively truth is an epistemic good even when
it is not justified. On JTB an unjustified true belief is not knowledge,
so with only Knowledge and Belief to name it it has to be named mere
Belief. It is therefore epistemically indistinguishable both from an
unjustified false belief and from a justified false belief, although we
want to say the true but unjustified believer is in a better position
than the false believer.

In other words JTB, with only the two names Knowledge and Belief
available, has no distinct place for a justified belief that is false and
no distinct place for a true belief that is unjustified. Both are forced
into the undifferentiated Belief category, so the account loses the
intuitive gradations of epistemic value between justified false
belief, unjustified true belief and plain false belief. That is the
justified-false-belief problem and the true-but-unjustified-belief / lucky
guess problem, the two non-Gettier cells left out of the JTB taxonomy.

* T & J & B  → Knowledge
* T & ~J & B  → ?
* ~T & J & B  → ?
